facts.claim: "Gears" was written by Joshua Allen Quimby.

"Gears" is track 4 on Joshua Quimby's self-titled album, released 22 April 2022 and credited ℗ 2022 Joshua Quimby. The album opens with "Ticket to Hartford" and also includes "To the Choir" and "Crescent Smile".
"Gears" was first put out as a standalone single dated 8 April 2022. It runs about 3:35 and Apple Music tags it folk-rock.
The lyrics of "Gears" deal with heavy marijuana use and self-medication.
Quimby recorded a live version, "Gears (OurVinyl Sessions)", which opens the 4-song "Joshua Quimby | OurVinyl Sessions" release of 19 July 2023.
Quimby says his self-titled debut is angstier, angrier and darker than the later "These Old Jeans" EP. He calls it a reflection of a more muddled, troubled mind.
Quimby was born in Rhode Island, raised in Connecticut, and now lives in Nashville.
Quimby moved to Nashville at 18, at first intending only to play guitar for other people before writing and recording his own music.
Quimby's second album, "Back Home" (May 2024), is a record about his New England roots. His influences include Bob Dylan, Hank Williams Sr. and John Prine.
His fourth album, "Piecemeal", came out 7 August 2026. It has ten songs and three poems, with features from Angela Autumn and Pompey.

draft:
Start with the thumb. In the first line of **Gears**, Joshua Quimby looks down and finds that "the tip of my thumb has been whittled like wood," worn down by the lighter he can't stop flicking. It's a funny image, and a little alarming. The habit has left a mark on the body, and he reports it the way you'd mention a callus from a guitar string. That mix of wry detail and quiet damage runs through the whole song.

Quimby wrote it alone, and the lyric is plain about what it covers: heavy marijuana use as self-medication. He knows the cure is part of the problem. He's smoking to put out a fire that the smoking keeps feeding. The second verse finds him on the floor of his room "in the company of constant concern," which is the loneliest line here. Worry is the only one keeping him company, and he can't even name where it comes from. Anyone who has felt anxious for no reason they could point to will know that floor.

The refrain ties two images together. The grass burns and the gears keep churning: the drug and the restless mind run side by side, and neither one wins. He calls it permanent, living and dying by the pipe, then hedges with "Least that's how it seems to me." That small doubt is the most hopeful moment in the song. It's fatalism with a crack in it. The last verse doesn't follow up on it, though. The closing line repeats three times, as if saying it enough could make it true.

The band plays against all that heaviness. An acoustic guitar strums at a moderate, swinging pace, a walking bass and steady drums keep things loose, and a fiddle threads a counter-melody around the voice with slides and double stops. The room sounds open and the mix is clean. Quimby sings alone, no harmonies, in a slightly raspy mid-range voice, and he delivers it straight. The easy groove sounds like the relief the reefer promises, which is the point and also the trap.

The folksy "a-tokin'," "a-burnin'" diction nods to the old-time vernacular of Hank Williams Sr. and the plainspoken humor of John Prine, both of whom Quimby names as influences. The rasp sits near Colter Wall. Quimby, who was raised in Connecticut and moved to Nashville at 18 meaning only to play guitar for others, has called this debut his angrier, darker record, the work of a muddled, troubled mind. "Gears" shows that mind without dressing it up.

It sticks because it makes the comfort and the trap sound like the same easy swing, so you sway along before you notice he's still on the floor.
